```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import textwrap

import circt
from circt import ir
from circt.dialects import arith, func
from circt.passmanager import PassManager


PASS_PIPELINE = "builtin.module(map-arith-to-comb)"


def register_dialects(context):
    circt.register_dialects(context)
    context.append_dialect_registry(arith.get_dialect_registry())
    context.append_dialect_registry(func.get_dialect_registry())
    context.load_all_available_dialects()


def build_integer_module():
    module = ir.Module.create()

    i1 = ir.IntegerType.get_signless(1)
    i8 = ir.IntegerType.get_signless(8)
    function_type = ir.FunctionType.get([i8, i8, i1], [i8])

    with ir.InsertionPoint(module.body):
        datapath = func.FuncOp("int_datapath", function_type)
        entry = datapath.add_entry_block()

        with ir.InsertionPoint(entry):
            a, b, select = entry.arguments

            sum_ = arith.addi(a, b)
            product = arith.muli(sum_, a)
            zero = arith.constant(i8, 0)

            product_is_positive = arith.cmpi(
                arith.CmpIPredicate.ugt,
                product,
                zero,
            )

            best = arith.select(
                product_is_positive,
                product,
                sum_,
            )

            result = arith.select(
                select,
                best,
                b,
            )

            func.return_([result])

    return module


FLOAT_EXAMPLE = """
module {
  func.func @float_datapath(%a: f32, %b: f32) -> f32 {
    %product = arith.mulf %a, %b : f32
    return %product : f32
  }
}
"""


def fenced(language, body):
    print(f"```{language}")
    print(textwrap.dedent(str(body)).strip())
    print("```")


def diagnostic(error, maximum_lines=16):
    lines = str(error).strip().splitlines()

    if len(lines) <= maximum_lines:
        return "\n".join(lines)

    return "\n".join(lines[:maximum_lines] + ["…"])
```

# Motivation {.section-title .center}

## Why MLIR for digital design? {auto-animate=true}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Software compiler view

```mlir
func.func @kernel(%a: i8, %b: i8) -> i8 {
  %sum = arith.addi %a, %b : i8
  return %sum : i8
}
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Hardware compiler view

```mlir
hw.module @Kernel(in %a: i8, in %b: i8, out y: i8) {
  %sum = comb.add %a, %b : i8
  hw.output %sum : i8
}
```
:::
:::

## Course objective {auto-animate=true}

::: {.callout-important}
Use MLIR and CIRCT to understand how arithmetic operations move from a generic
compiler representation to a hardware-oriented representation.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Build a small datapath with the CIRCT Python bindings.
- Apply a simple arithmetic-to-combinational lowering.
- Observe why integer operations lower but floating-point operations do not.
- Turn the limitation into a hands-on compiler exercise.
:::

## Pass used in this session {auto-animate=true}

```text
builtin.module(map-arith-to-comb)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The pass maps selected `arith` operations to `comb` operations. It is useful for
small examples and tests, not as a complete HLS flow.
:::

# Integer lowering {.section-title .center}

## Run the lowering {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| label: integer-lowering-run
#| output: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-3|5-6|8"

with ir.Context() as context, ir.Location.unknown():
    register_dialects(context)
    integer_module = build_integer_module()

    pass_manager = PassManager.parse(PASS_PIPELINE)
    pass_manager.run(integer_module.operation)

    lowered_integer_module = str(integer_module)
```

## Resulting IR {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| label: integer-lowering-result
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

fenced("mlir", lowered_integer_module)
```

## Key observation

::: {.incremental}
- The source contains `arith.addi`, `arith.muli`, `arith.cmpi`, and `arith.select`.
- The result contains `comb.add`, `comb.mul`, `comb.icmp`, and `comb.mux`.
- The lowering preserves the function boundary and the integer types.
:::

# Floating-point case {.section-title .center}

## Input IR {auto-animate=true}

```mlir
module {
  func.func @float_datapath(%a: f32, %b: f32) -> f32 {
    %product = arith.mulf %a, %b : f32
    return %product : f32
  }
}
```

## Run the same pass {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| label: float-lowering-run
#| output: false
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-3|5-6|8-15"

with ir.Context() as context, ir.Location.unknown():
    register_dialects(context)
    floating_point_module = ir.Module.parse(FLOAT_EXAMPLE)

    pass_manager = PassManager.parse(PASS_PIPELINE)

    try:
        pass_manager.run(floating_point_module.operation)
    except Exception as error:
        floating_point_result = diagnostic(error)
    else:
        floating_point_result = (
            "The pass completed without reporting an error.\n\n"
            + str(floating_point_module)
        )
```

## Diagnostic {auto-animate=true}

```{python}
#| label: float-lowering-result
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

fenced("text", floating_point_result)
```

## Why this becomes an exercise

::: {.callout-warning}
The demonstrated pass intentionally handles only a subset of arithmetic
lowering. Floating-point operations require an explicit representation and a
clear lowering policy.
:::

# Closing {.section-title .center}

## Takeaway

::: {.incremental}
- MLIR makes arithmetic explicit before hardware lowering.
- CIRCT provides hardware-oriented dialects such as `comb`.
- Small lowering passes are useful for understanding compiler structure.
- Unsupported operations are not only failures; they define the next compiler task.
:::
